newsitem.title: USA: Combining two similar drugs reduces HIV level in blood.
newsitem.headline: Combining two similar drugs reduces HIV level in blood.

text.p: Combining two similar drugs called protease inhibitors continues to show promise in reducing the HIV levels in patients after three months of studies, researchers reported on Monday.

Dr. Calvin J. Cohen, of Community Research Initiative of New England, said the second six weeks of tests using the two drugs showed even greater improvement than the first six weeks of tests. Those findings were released in July at the International AIDS Conference in Vancouver.

Speaking at the 36th Interscience Conference on Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, Cohen said the HIV viral load was reduced by 99.9 percent among patients given a combination of Abbott Laboratories' Novir (ritonavir) and Hoffmann-La Roche's Invirase (saquinavir mesylate).
The study involved 136 patients, divided into four groups, who were given different doses of the two drugs. About 7 percent discontinued the medication.

"The response in these dosing regimens demonstrates that saquinavir and retonavir appear to work synergistically," Cohen said. "These drugs interact in a way that clearly results in high therapeutic blood concentrations of both agents and increased antiviral activity."
Tingling around the mouth, diarrhoea, fatigue and nausea were the most commonly reported side effects and were generally mild, the report said.
Most of those who dropped out had been treated with 400 mgs of each drug three times a day. Cohen said reviews are being conducted to decide if that treatment regimen is warranted.
